metadata.title: Southwest Florida Plant Guide
metadata.description: Comprehensive plant reference guide for Southwest Florida covering native, beneficial non-native, edible, and invasive plants across 15 categories.

plants.description: The single most ecologically important tree you can plant in SW Florida. Supports hundreds of caterpillar and moth species — critical food for nesting birds. Acorns feed squirrels, deer, turkeys, blue jays, and woodpeckers year-round. Massive spreading canopy provides prime nesting sites for eagles, owls, and songbirds. Long-lived, hurricane resistant, and deeply beautiful. Give it significant room — it spreads as wide as it is tall.

Iconic tourist tree with striking peeling red-copper bark. One of SW Florida's fastest growing native trees and exceptionally hurricane resistant. Small fruits eaten by many birds. Extremely drought and salt tolerant. Great for quick canopy cover.

Native pine critical to Florida's flatwood ecosystem. Seeds eaten by doves, quail, squirrels, and many songbirds. Host tree for numerous moth and butterfly larvae. Essential cavity nesting sites for woodpeckers, owls, and flying squirrels. Perfectly suited to Cape Coral's well-drained sandy substrate.

Majestic native for wet areas, canal edges, and pond margins. Seeds eaten by wood ducks, sandhill cranes, and many birds. Important nesting habitat for ospreys, herons, and owls. Cypress knees create unique microhabitat. Stunning russet-orange fall color. Extremely long-lived.

Native holly producing masses of bright red berries that cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds devour in winter. Tolerates wet areas well. Can be grown as a large shrub or small tree. Female plants need a nearby male for berry production.
warnings: Berries are toxic to humans and pets — do not ingest.

plants.description: One of the most bird-attractive fruiting trees in Florida. Rose-breasted grosbeaks, scarlet tanagers, catbirds, and dozens of other species flock to it during fruiting in spring. Berries also eaten by raccoons, opossums, and foxes. Edible for humans — sweet and abundant.

Fast-growing native that works as a large shrub or small multi-trunk tree. Waxy gray berries are the primary winter food source for yellow-rumped warblers and many other migrating birds. Nitrogen-fixer that improves soil health. Highly salt tolerant and adaptable.

Native fruiting tree whose sweet fall fruits feed bluebirds, mockingbirds, warblers, raccoons, foxes, and deer. Edible for humans after fruits fully ripen — unripe fruits are very astringent. Host tree for luna moth and royal walnut moth caterpillars.
warnings: Unripe fruits are extremely astringent — wait until fully soft and ripe before eating.

plants.description: Evergreen native with blue-gray berries eaten by many birds — cedar waxwings are literally named for this tree. Dense fragrant foliage provides year-round nesting cover. Very salt and drought tolerant. Often protected under county tree ordinances.
warnings: Often protected by county ordinances — check local regulations before removing mature specimens.

plants.description: One of the most wildlife-productive trees in Florida — fruit eaten by 28+ bird species. Supports enormous insect diversity. Begins life as an epiphyte before becoming a freestanding tree. Protected tree in many FL counties.
warnings: Roots are very aggressive near hardscape and foundations. Plant well away from structures. Protected tree in many counties — check before removing.

plants.description: Classic coastal native highly tolerant of salt, wind, and drought. A keystone of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Can be maintained as a clipped formal hedge or allowed to grow into an attractive multi-trunk tree.

Iconic coastal native with huge round leathery leaves and grape-like fruit clusters. Fruits are edible for humans — used in jams and jellies — and eaten by many birds and mammals. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
warnings: Protected by Florida statute near coastlines — trimming may require permits. Check local regulations before pruning.

plants.description: One of SW Florida's most spectacular small native trees. Clusters of vivid orange trumpet flowers bloom nearly year-round and are a magnet for hummingbirds and bees. Very salt and drought tolerant. Stays relatively small at 15-25 ft — perfect for smaller yards.

Florida's native mahogany — a beautiful broad canopy tree of South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks. Seeds in large woody pods eaten by parrots and other birds. Host plant for several moth species. Semi-deciduous in late winter.

Small native tree with intensely fragrant golden-yellow puffball flowers in late winter and spring when little else is blooming — a critical early nectar source for bees and butterflies. Very drought tolerant. Thorny habit provides excellent protected nesting cover.
warnings: Has sharp thorns — plant away from high foot traffic areas.

plants.description: One of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — explosively covered in brilliant orange-red blooms in early summer. A defining tree of SW Florida's landscape. Fast-growing with a broad flat canopy providing excellent shade. Non-native but low ecological risk.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets if large quantities of seeds are ingested — monitor pets around fallen seed pods.

plants.description: Iconic tropical tree with intensely fragrant flowers in white, pink, yellow, red, and multicolor. One of the most planted ornamentals in SW Florida. Very drought tolerant. Goes briefly deciduous in winter.
warnings: Toxic to pets — milky sap causes vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation in dogs and cats. Keep pets away from fallen flowers and branches.

plants.description: Spectacular flowering trees that put on a jaw-dropping show of pink, yellow, or white trumpet blooms in spring — often before the leaves emerge. Bees and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Drought tolerant once established.

Very popular non-native with distinctive bright red brush-like flower spikes. Hummingbirds and bees adore the flowers. Drought and salt tolerant. Can be grown as a large shrub or trained into a multi-trunk tree up to 25 ft.

Extremely popular ornamental tree with showy summer blooms in pink, red, white, and purple. Bees visit the flowers actively. Attractive peeling bark and fall color. Very drought tolerant. One of the most commonly planted trees in SW Florida.
warnings: Avoid heavy topping — it destroys the natural form and weakens the tree. Prune lightly or not at all.

plants.description: Florida's state tree and a true ecological keystone. Berries are a critical food source for robins, cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, raccoons, and many other species. Old frond boots provide essential nesting habitat for owls, bats, and cavity-nesting birds. Highly fragrant flowers attract bees. Extremely hurricane and salt tolerant.
warnings: Edible heart-of-palm — but harvesting kills the tree. Never harvest from wild or landscape specimens.

plants.description: Arguably the most ecologically important shrub-palm in SW Florida. Berries are a critical food source for black bears, deer, raccoons, gopher tortoises, and dozens of bird species. Flowers are among Florida's most important bee plants. Dense colonies provide irreplaceable wildlife cover.
warnings: Serrated leaf stems cause cuts — handle with heavy gloves.

plants.description: Florida's most spectacular native palm — tall, straight, and regal with a smooth cement-gray trunk and a vivid green crownshaft. Small dark fruits eaten by many birds including parrots and pigeons. Fast growing for a palm. Surprisingly hurricane resistant.
warnings: Endangered in the wild — buy only nursery-grown specimens.

plants.description: The ultimate tropical icon. Coconuts are edible for humans and the fruits, flowers, and fronds all support wildlife. Very salt tolerant. Fast growing and striking. Available in Malayan dwarf varieties that stay lower and produce earlier.
warnings: Falling coconuts are a genuine hazard — plant away from seating areas, walkways, and parked cars. Remove nuts regularly in high-traffic areas.

plants.description: Not actually a palm at all — a cycad. Extremely popular in SW Florida landscapes for its neat symmetrical form. However it is one of the most dangerously toxic plants to dogs and cats in existence. Virtually no wildlife value.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — one of the most poisonous plants to pets in Florida. All parts are toxic; seeds are extremely dangerous and can cause liver failure and death in dogs and cats. Avoid entirely if pets have yard access.

plants.description: The king of SW Florida fruit trees. Thrives in Cape Coral's heat and humidity. Grafted trees fruit in 2-3 years. Prune annually after harvest to control size and promote production. Watch for anthracnose fungal disease during wet season.
warnings: Mango sap and skin can cause skin irritation in sensitive people. Mango pit and skin can cause digestive issues in pets — keep pits away from dogs.

varieties.name: Carrie
varieties.notes: One of the best backyard varieties — compact tree, incredibly rich flavor, no fiber. Self-pollinating. Early harvest May-June.

varieties.name: Cogshall
varieties.notes: Top condo mango — slow growing, very easy to control size. Perfect for small yards or containers. Fiberless, excellent flavor.

varieties.name: Nam Doc Mai
varieties.notes: Thai variety with sweet fragrant fiber-free fruit. Semi-dwarf, manageable size. July-August harvest.

varieties.name: Kent
varieties.notes: Considered one of the sweetest Florida mangoes. Large tree but excellent production. Late season harvest July-August.

varieties.name: Keitt
varieties.notes: Best late season variety — stays green when ripe. Large fruit, heat tolerant, excellent disease resistance. Harvest August-September.

plants.description: Excellent fruit tree for SW Florida in well-drained spots. West Indian varieties are best suited to Cape Coral's heat. Needs good drainage. Plant Type A and Type B varieties together for best pollination. Watch for laurel wilt disease.
warnings: Toxic to pets — the leaves, bark, skin, and pit contain persin which causes vomiting and diarrhea in dogs and cats. Keep fallen fruit picked up.

varieties.name: Choquette
varieties.notes: One of the most popular Florida backyard varieties. Large fruit up to 3 lbs, good flavor. Harvest November-January.

varieties.name: Monroe
varieties.notes: Large high-quality fruit with excellent flavor. Good disease resistance. Pairs well with Choquette for cross-pollination.

varieties.name: Brogdon
varieties.notes: Most cold-tolerant Florida variety. Medium fruit, good flavor. Harvest August-October.

varieties.name: Hall
varieties.notes: Excellent disease resistance — recommended by UF/IFAS. Good flavor, medium-large fruit. Harvest October-November.

varieties.name: Lula
varieties.notes: Classic Florida variety, cold tolerant, good production. Medium fruit with rich flavor. Harvest October-December.

plants.description: One of the best all-around wildlife shrubs for Southwest Florida. Tubular red-orange flowers bloom nearly year-round attracting hummingbirds and butterflies constantly. Dark berries eaten by many bird species. Host plant for the pluto sphinx moth. Important: only plant the true native Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf, African, or compacta varieties.
warnings: Do NOT buy dwarf, African, or compacta varieties — they are not native and have significantly less wildlife value.

plants.description: Famous for its extraordinary clusters of metallic purple berries eaten by over 40 bird species and deer. Host plant for spring azure butterfly. Low maintenance — dies back and rebounds vigorously each season. Adaptable to sun through shade.

Widely planted for extraordinary drought and salt tolerance, fast growth, and showy flowers in pink, white, red, and yellow. However the toxicity is severe and demands serious thought before planting in home landscapes with children or pets.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts including sap, flowers, leaves, stems, and water in a vase containing oleander are extremely toxic to humans, pets, horses, and livestock. Smoke from burning branches is toxic. One of the most dangerous common landscape plants.

plants.description: One of the most essential hummingbird and butterfly plants for Southwest Florida. Brilliant red spikes bloom nearly year-round. Self-seeds prolifically so you will always have more. Very drought tolerant and easy. Excellent companion to firebush and blue porterweed.

Florida's single best lawn-substitute groundcover. Host plant for common buckeye, phaon crescent, and white peacock butterflies. Tiny white-purple flowers attract native bees constantly. Seeds eaten by birds. Can be mowed. Handles light foot traffic. One of the most ecologically valuable plants per square foot in all of Southwest Florida.

One of the absolute best native vines for Southwest Florida. Tubular red and orange flowers bloom nearly year-round and hummingbirds are completely unable to resist them. Red berries eaten by birds. Well-behaved unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle. A must-have for any hummingbird garden.

One of the most beloved native grasses in Florida. In fall the clouds of airy pink-purple flower plumes are absolutely stunning — glowing in late afternoon light. Seeds eaten by birds. Dense clumps provide cover for ground birds and lizards. Plant in drifts for maximum impact.

The single most recommended native aquatic plant for Southwest Florida's canals, ponds, and wet areas. Vivid violet-blue flower spikes bloom nearly year-round. Bees and butterflies visit constantly. Seeds eaten by ducks and water birds. Dense colonies provide critical fish habitat. Edible — seeds eaten like buckwheat, young leaves cooked like spinach.

The most iconic epiphyte of the American South. Not a moss, not a parasite — a true flowering bromeliad. Critical nesting material for northern parulas, Baltimore orioles, and other birds. Indicator of clean air quality. Harmless to healthy trees. A living symbol of authentic Florida.
warnings: Spanish moss often harbors chiggers and redbugs — wear long sleeves and gloves when handling fresh fallen clumps.

plants.description: Florida's most common native cactus and an ecological powerhouse. Large showy yellow flowers with red centers attract bees and butterflies. Red-purple fruits eaten by gopher tortoises, birds, deer, and small mammals. Entire plant is edible — pads, fruits, and flowers all used in cooking. Very drought and salt tolerant.
warnings: Glochids — tiny barbed bristles on pads and fruits — cause intense skin irritation and are nearly invisible. Always wear thick gloves when handling.

plants.description: Florida's largest native terrestrial fern — bold arching fronds can reach 6-8 ft creating a dramatic tropical statement. Excellent groundcover under trees and in shaded areas. Provides dense wildlife cover for frogs, lizards, and ground birds. Very fast growing once established. Pet safe.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive tuberous sword fern (N. cordifolia) or Asian sword fern (N. brownii). Native giant sword fern has double-toothed pinnae margins and no tubers on runners. Always verify scientific name at purchase.

plants.description: One of Southwest Florida's most magical native plants — white to pink lily flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer rains. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Naturalizes beautifully in lawns and garden beds spreading over time. A classic Florida native experience.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — bulbs especially dangerous containing lycorine alkaloids. Do not ingest.

plants.description: Arguably the single most ecologically important weed in Florida. Butterflies and native bees swarm it constantly all year long — documented as one of the top three most important honeybee plants in the Southeast. Seeds eaten by birds. Edible leaves and flowers used as salad garnish. Let it grow wherever you can.
plants.management: Let grow freely or manage after blooming to limit spread. Worth keeping in every yard.

plants.description: The single most destructive invasive plant in Southwest Florida. Forms impenetrable dense thickets that completely displace native vegetation. Red berries look attractive but are mildly toxic and the tree provides almost no native wildlife value compared to the habitat it destroys. Now covers over 700,000 acres in South Florida. Remove immediately whenever found.
warnings: Sap causes severe skin and eye irritation — related to poison ivy. Wear gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves when handling. Berries toxic to pets. Smoke from burning is toxic.
plants.removal_method: Cut stems at ground level and immediately apply concentrated herbicide (triclopyr or glyphosate) to cut surface. DO NOT burn — smoke is toxic. Repeat treatments needed. Root system must be killed or it resprouts. Contact Lee or Collier County Extension for assistance.

plants.description: Australian tree that has invaded over 500,000 acres of South Florida's wetlands. Drains wetlands by transpiring enormous amounts of water, converting sawgrass marshes and cypress swamps into melaleuca monocultures. Federally listed noxious weed. Remove immediately.
warnings: Do not burn standing melaleuca — heat triggers seed release from the canopy. One tree can release millions of seeds when burned.
plants.removal_method: Cut and immediately treat stump with concentrated herbicide. Hack and squirt method effective on larger trees. Biological control (Melaleuca snout beetle) available — contact SFWMD for current programs.

plants.description: Free-floating plant from South America that can double its population in two weeks, completely choking canals, ponds, and waterways. Reduces oxygen in water killing fish. Blocks boat traffic. Has infested Florida waterways since the 1880s and costs the state millions annually to control. Never introduce to water features.
warnings: Removal requires permits for aquatic herbicide use in Florida waterways. Contact SFWMD before applying any chemical treatment to canals.
plants.removal_method: Physical removal by hand or equipment for small infestations. Aquatic herbicides (2,4-D, glyphosate labeled for aquatic use) for larger infestations — requires permits. Contact SFWMD for assistance with canal infestations.

plants.description: Underused native understory tree related to blueberry. Delicate bell-shaped white spring flowers feed bees. Shiny blue-black fall berries attract birds. Bark flakes to reveal attractive reddish layers. Well adapted to Florida's sandy soils.
Native coastal hammock tree with clusters of small grape-like fruits beloved by white-crowned pigeons and mockingbirds. Edible for humans — small and tart. Very salt and drought tolerant.

Attractive native hammock tree with glossy pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits that many birds eat. Fast-growing and good for quick canopy. Interesting compound leaves give a tropical appearance.

Often overlooked but highly valuable native coastal hammock tree. Small red fruits are an important food source for migrating warblers and vireos. One of the few native trees that tolerates shade well. Very salt tolerant.

Enormously productive in SW Florida. Leaves, pods, seeds, and flowers all edible and highly nutritious. Grows extremely fast. Straight trunks useful as garden stakes. Prune hard regularly to keep productive and manageable.
warnings: Leaves typically eaten cooked or dried rather than raw in large quantities.

plants.description: Breathtaking tree with clouds of lavender-purple tubular flowers in spring. Feathery fern-like foliage attractive even when not in bloom. Less salt tolerant so better for inland properties. Not invasive in FL.

One of the most commonly planted shade trees in SW Florida. Dense evergreen canopy provides excellent shade and bird nesting habitat. Very hurricane resistant. Salt and drought tolerant. Slow growing but extremely long-lived.
Stunning ornamental with large velvety deep purple flowers and soft fuzzy leaves. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit frequently. Not salt tolerant — better for inland properties.
Spectacular tree cascading with long hanging clusters of bright yellow flowers in spring. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers actively. Birds eat the seeds.
warnings: Toxic to pets and livestock — all parts especially seed pods are toxic. The pulp is used medicinally but should never be self-administered.

plants.description: Distinctive multi-trunk clumping native palm of the Everglades and SW Florida wetlands. Small black fruits eaten by birds and small mammals. Dense clumps provide excellent nesting and shelter. Tolerates periodic flooding well — excellent for low spots and canal edges.
Elegant native fan palm with a slender trunk and graceful crown. Small white fruits eaten by birds. Very salt and drought tolerant. Fragrant flowers attract bees.
warnings: Threatened species — purchase only from reputable nurseries growing legally propagated specimens.

plants.description: The world's most cold-hardy palm — native to Florida. Low clumping growth with vicious needle-like spines makes it impenetrable cover for ground-nesting birds. Shade tolerant — one of very few palms that grows well in partial to full shade.
warnings: Extremely sharp needle-like spines can cause serious injury to people and pets. Plant away from foot traffic and pet areas.

plants.description: One of the most popular privacy screening palms in SW Florida. Clumping multi-stem growth creates a dense lush hedge quickly. Birds nest in the dense fronds and eat the small fruits. Requires regular fertilization in FL's sandy soils.
warnings: Listed as caution for invasive potential in South Florida by UF/IFAS — plant where fruit drop can be managed.

plants.description: One of the most popular ornamental palms in SW Florida. Compact, clean, self-cleaning, and produces clusters of vivid red fruits in December. No nutrient deficiency issues that plague queen and foxtail palms. Excellent for smaller yards.

Visually striking palm with distinctive plume-like fronds. Very popular in SW Florida despite being poorly adapted to local conditions. Prone to chronic nutrient deficiency in sandy coastal soils. Not salt tolerant.
warnings: Toxic to pets — fruits, fronds, and bark contain toxic compounds. Keep pets away from fallen fruits. Also poorly suited to SW Florida's coastal sandy soils — prone to nutrient deficiency and decline.

plants.description: One of the most rewarding fruit trees for SW Florida — the climate here is genuinely ideal. Needs a slightly cool dry winter to trigger flowering. Not salt tolerant — avoid coastal beachfront sites. Slow to start but very long-lived and productive.
warnings: Lychee seeds and unripe fruit contain hypoglycin-like compounds toxic to pets. Keep pets away from fallen fruit and seeds.

varieties.name: Mauritius
varieties.notes: The most widely recommended and reliable lychee for Florida. Consistent producer, good flavor, bright red fruit.

varieties.name: Brewster
varieties.notes: Large attractive fruit, very heavy producer in good years.

varieties.name: Sweetheart
varieties.notes: Small seed means more edible flesh. Excellent sweet flavor.

varieties.name: Emperor
varieties.notes: Newer variety producing very large fruit. Growing in popularity.

plants.description: One of the most productive and easy fruit trees for SW Florida. Produces multiple crops per year. Sweet varieties are excellent fresh eating. Very ornamental with pretty pink flowers.
warnings: Toxic to people with kidney disease. For pets, starfruit is toxic to dogs and cats — keep fallen fruit picked up.

varieties.name: Arkin
varieties.notes: Most widely planted sweet variety in Florida. Large fruit, excellent flavor, very productive.

varieties.name: Fwang Tung
varieties.notes: Very sweet Thai variety, large fruit, multiple crops per year.

varieties.name: Kary
varieties.notes: More compact tree size than Arkin — good for smaller yards.

plants.description: Exceptionally well suited to SW Florida — one of the most salt and drought tolerant fruit trees available. Sweet brown fruit with a flavor like brown sugar, pear, and vanilla combined. Very ornamental with glossy evergreen foliage.

varieties.name: Prolific
varieties.notes: Most widely planted sapodilla in Florida. Very heavy crops, good consistent flavor.

varieties.name: Tikal
varieties.notes: Larger fruit than Prolific with excellent rich flavor.

varieties.name: Alano
varieties.notes: Classic Florida variety, very heavy producer. Large tree — needs space.

plants.description: Extremely productive and easy fruit tree for SW Florida. Produces abundantly with minimal care. Rich in vitamin C. Birds and wildlife eagerly eat the fruit.
warnings: Common guava can become invasive in natural areas of South Florida — plant where fruit drop is managed and do not plant near natural areas or preserves.

varieties.name: Tropical White
varieties.notes: Most popular backyard guava in Florida. White flesh, mild sweet tropical flavor.

varieties.name: Ruby Supreme
varieties.notes: Pink-red flesh with richer, stronger flavor. Excellent for juice and guava paste.

varieties.name: Homestead
varieties.notes: Florida-developed variety well adapted to local conditions.

plants.description: Florida is citrus country and SW Florida grows it well. Citrus trees are also important host plants for giant swallowtail butterflies. Needs well-drained soil and full sun. Fertilize regularly with citrus-specific fertilizer.
warnings: Citrus fruit flesh is mildly toxic to dogs and cats due to citric acid. Note: citrus canker and greening (HLB) are serious diseases in Florida — buy disease-free certified nursery stock only.

varieties.name: Meyer lemon
varieties.notes: Most popular backyard citrus in SW Florida. Sweeter than standard lemon, nearly thornless, compact.

varieties.name: Hamlin orange
varieties.notes: Best sweet orange for South Florida. Early season, heavy crops, good flavor.

varieties.name: Ruby red grapefruit
varieties.notes: Best grapefruit for SW Florida. Sweet pink flesh, very productive.

varieties.name: Honey tangerine / Murcott
varieties.notes: One of the sweetest and most flavorful tangerines available.

plants.description: One of the fastest fruit producers available — can fruit in less than a year from planting. Very productive year-round. Short-lived but self-seeds readily. Needs good drainage despite needing regular water.

varieties.name: Red Lady
varieties.notes: Most widely recommended backyard papaya. Compact plant, red-orange flesh, very sweet flavor. Disease resistant.

varieties.name: Maradol
varieties.notes: Large fruit with rich red flesh, commercial quality flavor.

varieties.name: Solo / Sunrise
varieties.notes: Small individual-serving size fruit. Very sweet golden-orange flesh.

plants.description: Outstanding native understory shrub with glossy quilted leaves, small white flowers, and bright red berries eaten by many birds. Host plant for several hairstreak butterflies. One of the best shade-tolerant native shrubs.

Excellent multi-purpose native shrub or small tree. Fragrant white flowers attract bees; orange-red berries are a top food source for mockingbirds, robins, and cedar waxwings. One of the most reliable and rewarding native shrubs.

Spectacular native hibiscus with enormous brilliant scarlet star-shaped flowers that hummingbirds spot from across the yard. Grows in wet areas, pond edges, and rain gardens. Can reach 6-8 ft tall. Dies back in winter and returns vigorously in spring.

One of the most wildlife-productive native shrubs in North America. Distinctive white pincushion-like fragrant flowers attract hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies in huge numbers. Seeds eaten by ducks and wetland birds. Essential for pond edges and canal banks.
warnings: All parts contain cephalanthin — toxic to pets, livestock, and humans if ingested. Despite toxicity it is one of the most ecologically valuable native shrubs available.

plants.description: One of the absolute best non-native butterfly and hummingbird shrubs for Southwest Florida. Dense clusters of star-shaped flowers in red, pink, white, and lavender bloom year-round. Butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds use it constantly.
One of the most spectacular flowering plants in Southwest Florida. Cascading bracts in magenta, orange, white, red, and purple. Extremely drought tolerant. Blooms better with less water.
warnings: Thorns cause skin punctures — wear gloves when pruning. Sap can cause mild skin irritation in sensitive people and pets.

plants.description: One of the best non-native hummingbird and butterfly shrubs for Southwest Florida. Long spikes of vivid scarlet-red tubular flowers bloom year-round. One of very few red-flowering plants that performs well in partial to full shade — a rare and valuable trait.
See main oleander entry. White-flowered variety. Same extraordinary drought and salt tolerance, same severe toxicity.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts extremely toxic to humans, pets, horses, and livestock. Smoke from burning branches is toxic.

plants.description: Low-growing perennial with vivid blue flower spikes that hummingbirds, butterflies, and bees adore. Blooms continuously year-round. Host plant for several skipper butterflies. Salt and drought tolerant.

Fast-growing cheerful native sunflower that blooms year-round. Seeds beloved by goldfinches, doves, and sparrows. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers constantly. Extremely drought and salt tolerant.
Native milkweed and the ecologically correct host plant for monarch and queen butterflies. Brilliant orange flowers. Prefers well-drained sandy soil — perfect for Cape Coral's natural substrate.
warnings: Milkweed family — contains cardiac glycosides. Mildly toxic to pets in large quantities.

plants.description: One of the absolute best non-native butterfly flowers available. Large showy blooms visited constantly by swallowtails, monarchs, sulfurs, and many other butterflies. Very easy annual — direct sow in the garden.

Heat-loving perennial that thrives in Southwest Florida. Large tropical blooms in red, orange, yellow, and pink nearly year-round. Hummingbirds and bees visit regularly. Edible rhizomes used like arrowroot.

Extremely popular annual in SW Florida for its heat tolerance and nearly constant blooms. Butterflies and bees visit actively. Very drought tolerant. Despite being common at every garden center it is genuinely dangerous to pets.
warnings: Toxic to pets and humans — all parts contain vinca alkaloids which can cause serious neurological symptoms including nerve damage, tremors, and in large amounts death.

plants.description: Spectacular tropical perennial with bold architectural flowers in vivid red, orange, and yellow that hummingbirds love. Large banana-like leaves provide bold tropical texture. Spreads by rhizomes to form impressive clumps.
Low-growing native with fluffy pink powderpuff flowers that close when touched. Host plant for little sulphur butterfly. Nitrogen-fixer improving sandy soil. Handles light foot traffic.
Florida's only native cycad and the sole host plant for the atala butterfly — a species that nearly went extinct without it. Essentially indestructible once established. Handles sun to full shade.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — seeds especially dangerous. Despite toxicity, ecologically irreplaceable.

plants.description: One of the most widely used non-native groundcovers in SW Florida. Dense low evergreen mat. Extremely adaptable — sun to full shade, drought tolerant, salt tolerant.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets if ingested. Despite being widely planted as a safe groundcover, keep pets from grazing on it.

plants.description: One of the best non-native lawn alternatives approved by UF/IFAS Florida Friendly Landscaping. Continuous bright yellow flowers attract bees and butterflies. Nitrogen-fixer requiring no synthetic fertilizer. Can be mowed every 4-8 weeks.

One of the most ecologically important native vines in Florida. Host plant for gulf fritillary, zebra longwing (Florida's state butterfly), and julia butterflies — essential for their survival. Stunning intricate purple flowers. Edible fruits for humans.
Native vine whose berries are eaten by over 35 bird species. Host plant for several sphinx moths and butterfly species. Adapts to sun through shade. Stunning red fall color.
warnings: Berries are toxic to humans and pets — can cause kidney damage if ingested.

plants.description: One of the most popular vines in Southwest Florida — the fragrance of the white pinwheel flowers in spring is extraordinary. Bees and butterflies visit actively. Evergreen year-round. Very drought tolerant. Pet safe per ASPCA.
Instant tropical drama with large trumpet flowers in vivid red, pink, and white blooming nearly non-stop. Hummingbirds and bees visit actively. Very popular for porches and trellises.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — sap causes skin irritation and ingestion causes mild gastrointestinal upset.

plants.description: Non-native passionvine grown for its delicious edible fruit. Like its native cousin, it is also a host plant for gulf fritillary and other longwing butterflies. Very productive in Southwest Florida's climate.
Large evergreen native grass with bold arching dark green leaves. Seeds eaten by ground-foraging birds. Host plant for several skipper butterflies. Dense clumps provide excellent wildlife cover.
Iconic coastal grass that holds Florida's beach dunes together. Dramatic golden seed heads eaten by birds. Essential for coastal dune stabilization.
warnings: Protected by Florida law — it is illegal to pick, transplant, or damage sea oats on public beaches or dunes. Buy only nursery-grown specimens.

plants.description: Striking native sedge with distinctive white-tipped bracts that look like a starburst. Attracts bees and small butterflies. Seeds eaten by birds. Excellent for rain gardens and moist low spots.
Evergreen native rush for wet areas, canal edges, and pond margins. Dense clumps provide excellent nesting habitat for marsh birds, frogs, and small mammals.
Large clumping grass with aromatic stalks widely used in cooking. Very drought tolerant. Dual purpose as both ornamental landscape grass and productive kitchen herb.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — essential oils can cause gastrointestinal upset. Not severely dangerous but monitor if pets chew on it.

plants.description: Native emergent with distinctive arrow-shaped leaves and white three-petaled flowers. Starchy tubers eaten by ducks, wading birds, muskrats, and historically by Native Americans. Important fish habitat plant.
Dramatic architectural native with large paddle-shaped leaves on tall stalks and airy purple flower clusters. Creates a bold tropical statement along canal banks and pond margins.
Florida's native white water lily with intensely fragrant flowers. Floating leaves shade the water reducing algae. Provides important fish habitat and cover.
Stunning native iris with large blue-violet flowers in spring. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit actively. Dense clumps provide excellent nesting cover for marsh birds and frogs.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — rhizomes especially dangerous. Can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation. Do not ingest.

plants.description: Low-growing native aquatic herb with small white flowers blooming year-round. Bees and butterflies visit. Important in Ayurvedic medicine. Very adaptable to wet soil through shallow water.
warnings: Medicinal herb — used in Ayurvedic medicine but should not be self-administered without professional guidance.

plants.description: Florida's largest commonly seen tillandsia. Tank bromeliad whose central cup holds water providing habitat for tree frogs, insects, and nesting birds. Hummingbirds visit the flowers.
warnings: Endangered — protected by Florida law. Only purchase from licensed nurseries growing legally propagated specimens. Never collect from the wild.
plants.mount_method: Wire to tree bark or cork

plants.description: One of nature's most remarkable plants — can lose 97% of its water content appearing completely dead and brown, then fully resurrect to vivid green within hours of rain. Forms carpets on live oak branches.

Florida's most common and accessible native epiphytic orchid. Clusters of yellow-green to brown flowers — fragrant and beautiful. Found naturally on live oaks. Mount on cork bark or attach to a large oak branch.
plants.mount_method: Mount on cork bark or tree branches

plants.description: Spectacular non-native epiphytic fern with distinctive antler-shaped fronds. No significant wildlife value but provides some microhabitat. Very popular in Southwest Florida's warm climate.
plants.mount_method: Mount on wood board or attach to tree

plants.description: One of the rarest and most special plants in this entire guide — a columnar cactus endemic to Southwest Florida and found nowhere else on earth. Large fragrant white night-blooming flowers attract sphinx moths and hummingbirds.
warnings: Endangered and endemic to Southwest Florida — found only in Lee and Sarasota counties in the world. Protected by Florida law. Purchase only from licensed nurseries. Spines cause injury — handle with care.

plants.description: Spectacular vining cactus producing enormous night-blooming white flowers and delicious pink or white-fleshed fruits. Thrives in Southwest Florida's tropical climate. Needs support to climb.
warnings: Night-blooming — flowers open only one night each year per bloom. Multiple plants or hand pollination recommended for fruit production.

plants.description: One of the most useful plants in existence — the clear gel inside the leaves is a renowned treatment for burns and skin irritation. Hummingbirds visit the tubular orange flower spikes.
warnings: Toxic to pets — ingestion causes vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, and changes in urine color in dogs and cats. Gel is safe for external use but ingestion is toxic.

plants.description: Compact rosette succulents in a stunning range of colors and forms. One of the most popular succulent genera and one of the most pet safe. Excellent ornamental plants for containers, rock gardens, and dry sunny spots.
The original wild ancestor of the cultivated Boston fern. Grows naturally in hammocks and along fence lines throughout Southwest Florida. Provides excellent ground-level cover for wildlife.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive tuberous sword fern (N. cordifolia). The native wild form has simple toothed pinnae.

plants.description: One of the most striking native plants in Southwest Florida — enormous fronds can reach 12 ft. The largest fern in North America. Very salt tolerant. Provides critical nesting habitat for wading birds.
Native fern of wet hammocks, swamp edges, and canal margins throughout Southwest Florida. Very adaptable to sun through shade. Forms dense colonies providing excellent ground-level cover.
Classic native fern with distinctive cinnamon-colored fertile fronds. Birds use the woolly fiber at the base for nesting material. Excellent for rain gardens and moist shaded areas.

Stunning native bulb with dramatic fragrant white spider-like flowers. Hummingbirds, bees, and large butterflies visit. Very salt tolerant — one of the best flowering natives for coastal properties. Self-seeds readily to form colonies.
warnings: Bulbs toxic to humans and pets — contain lycorine. Always wear gloves when handling bulbs.

plants.description: Native bulb of wet hammocks producing spectacular fragrant white flowers with prominent pink stamens. Host plant for Spanish moth caterpillars. Perfect for canal edges and pond margins.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — bulbs especially dangerous.

plants.description: One of the most productive and easy edible rhizomes for Southwest Florida. Bright orange roots are the turmeric spice. Thrives in Southwest Florida's heat as a perennial. Beautiful pink and white flower spikes in summer.
Fresh ginger thrives as a perennial in Southwest Florida's warm humid climate. Rhizomes harvested after leaves die back. Very productive — one planted rhizome produces many more.
Tropical plant producing starchy edible tubers used as a thickening agent in cooking. Thrives in Southwest Florida's warm climate as a perennial.
Spectacular large trumpet flowers in red, pink, white, and striped combinations. Hummingbirds and bees visit. Very easy in Southwest Florida — goes semi-dormant in summer and re-blooms reliably.
warnings: All parts toxic to pets — contain lycorine causing vomiting, diarrhea, and low blood pressure. Bulbs are the most toxic part.

plants.description: Extraordinarily beautiful vine-like lily with dramatic swept-back flame-colored petals. Despite extraordinary beauty the toxicity is severe.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts contain colchicine which can cause serious multi-organ failure in pets and humans. Even small amounts are extremely dangerous. Only grow in completely inaccessible areas.

plants.description: Low pink-flowered native that spreads through lawns. Host plant for little sulphur butterfly. Nitrogen-fixer improving soil. Goes dormant in winter. One of the best lawn alternatives for sunny spots.
plants.management: Let spread freely in sunny areas. Can be mowed.

plants.description: Purple-flowered native that spreads through beds and lawn edges. Host plant for three butterfly species. Blooms nearly year-round. Adaptable from full sun to shade.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive Mexican petunia (Ruellia simplex) — check leaf size and invasive status before removing any Ruellia.
plants.management: Let grow where found or transplant to garden beds.

plants.description: Beautiful purple-flowered plant that looks like native wild petunia but is a Category 1 invasive. Spreads aggressively into natural areas by seeds that pop explosively. All varieties including Purple Showers are invasive.
plants.management: REMOVE if present. Replace with native wild petunia (Ruellia caroliniensis).

plants.description: Vine from Asia that grows explosively — up to 8 inches per day — smothering trees and shrubs. Produces aerial bulbils that drop and sprout new plants. Virtually impossible to fully eradicate without sustained multi-year effort.
warnings: Bulbils toxic to pets and humans if ingested. Grows up to 8 inches per day in summer.
plants.removal_method: Collect and destroy ALL aerial bulbils — bag and dispose in trash, never compost. Cut vines at ground level and treat with herbicide. Biological control beetle (Lilioceris cheni) available.

plants.description: Climbing fern from Asia that smothers trees and shrubs with lacy fronds, climbing 100+ ft into tree canopies. Forms dense mats that carry fire into tree canopies dramatically increasing fire intensity. Federally listed noxious weed.
warnings: Federally listed noxious weed. Spores spread by wind — can invade natural areas from miles away.
plants.removal_method: Herbicide (metsulfuron-methyl) most effective. Cut and treat cut ends. Contact SFWMD for guidance.

plants.description: Australian tree that forms dense monocultures on coastal dunes eliminating sea turtle nesting habitat. Produces allelopathic leaf litter preventing other plants from growing beneath it. Illegal to plant in Florida.
warnings: Removal may require permits in some counties — check with Lee or Collier County before removing large specimens.
plants.removal_method: Cut and immediately treat stump with triclopyr. Root system must be killed.

plants.description: Asian grass that is one of the world's worst invasive weeds. Forms dense monocultures that nothing eats, nothing nests in. Highly flammable. Federally listed noxious weed.
warnings: Federally listed noxious weed. Report new infestations to FDACS (1-888-397-1517). Highly flammable — creates intense fast-moving fires. Do not mow — spreads rhizome fragments.
plants.removal_method: Repeated herbicide applications (imazapyr or glyphosate) over multiple seasons. Cannot be mowed out.

plants.description: Asian shrub planted widely as an ornamental that now invades hammocks and shaded understory. Forms dense colonies shading out native understory plants. Very commonly sold at nurseries despite invasive status.
warnings: Berries toxic to pets. Frequently confused with native marlberry — check leaf edges (serrated = invasive, smooth = native marlberry).
plants.removal_method: Dig out by hand including roots. Bag and dispose of all berries. Very important to remove before berries drop.

plants.description: Grass from Asia that has invaded pastures, wetlands, and canal banks throughout Southwest Florida. Spreads aggressively by deep rhizomes and floating stem fragments carried by water. Forms dense monocultures providing no wildlife value.
warnings: Spreads through water movement — rhizome fragments float and establish downstream. Very difficult to eradicate once established near canals.
plants.removal_method: Repeated glyphosate applications over multiple seasons. Very difficult — rhizomes extend deep and wide.

plants.description: Floating rosette plant that forms dense mats on ponds and canals, blocking sunlight, reducing oxygen, and destroying fish habitat. Spreads rapidly in warm weather. Very common in Southwest Florida's canals.
warnings: Toxic to pets if ingested. Requires permits for chemical removal in waterways.
plants.removal_method: Physical removal and disposal. Aquatic herbicide with permit. Can be composted but do not return any fragments to water.

plants.description: Submerged aquatic plant from Asia that forms dense canopies at the water surface, blocking sunlight and killing native aquatic vegetation. Federally listed noxious weed costing Florida over $30 million per year to manage.
warnings: Federally listed noxious weed. Chemical removal requires state permits. Report new water body infestations to SFWMD.
plants.removal_method: Aquatic herbicide (fluridone, diquat) with SFWMD permit required. Contact SFWMD — this is a managed species at the state level.

plants.description: Spectacular African tree with large orange-red trumpet flowers widely planted and still sold in SW Florida. Despite its beauty it is a Category 1 invasive — and critically, its nectar is toxic to native bees.
warnings: Nectar is toxic to native bees — the flowers look appealing for wildlife but actively poison bee populations. Do not plant thinking it has pollinator value.
plants.removal_method: Cut and treat stump with triclopyr immediately. Produces winged seeds spread by wind. Remove all seedlings promptly.

plants.description: Widely sold as an ornamental that escapes into natural areas and hammocks forming dense colonies displacing native ferns and groundcovers. Toxic berries spread by birds.
warnings: Toxic to pets — berries cause vomiting and diarrhea. Do NOT confuse with foxtail fern (Asparagus densiflorus Meyersii) — foxtail fern is not invasive but the standard asparagus fern absolutely is.
plants.removal_method: Dig out including tubers — tubers resprout if left. Bag all material. Multiple removal sessions needed.

plants.description: One of the most commonly planted palms in SW Florida — but now classified as a Category 2 invasive that is escaping into natural areas of South Florida per Naples Botanical Garden.
warnings: Category 2 invasive per Naples Botanical Garden — invading natural areas in South Florida. Despite widespread use in landscaping it is escaping.
plants.removal_method: Remove by cutting — stumps do not resprout. Collect all fallen fruits before they germinate. Monitor for seedlings.

plants.description: Stunning ornamental tree with large orchid-like purple-pink flowers that bloom in fall and winter — a welcome burst of color when little else is blooming. Sterile hybrid so does not set seed — no invasive risk. Very popular in SW Florida landscapes.

Iconic symmetrical conifer widely planted in SW Florida as a living Christmas tree and landscape specimen. Very salt tolerant. Birds nest in the branches and eat seeds from cones. Grows tall and narrow — good for tight spaces.
warnings: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs — can cause vomiting and lethargy if needles are ingested.

plants.description: Tropical tree with intensely fragrant yellow-green star-shaped flowers used in perfumery — the scent is extraordinary. Blooms nearly year-round. Bees and hummingbirds visit. Grows very fast into a large weeping-form tree.
Small elegant native fan palm native to southern Florida and the Keys. Shiny white pea-sized fruits relished by wildlife. Very salt and drought tolerant. Stays relatively small at 15-20 ft.
warnings: Rare in cultivation — may be difficult to source. Seek out Florida native plant nurseries.

plants.description: Striking small native palm with silvery-blue undersides to the fan-shaped leaves. Small dark fruits eaten by birds. Extremely salt and drought tolerant. Stays small and slender — perfect for smaller yards or accent planting.
Small clumping fan palm that is one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant non-native palms available. Dense multi-trunk clumps provide good bird nesting cover. Stays small and tidy.

Lush low-growing clumping palm excellent for shaded areas where most palms won't grow. One of very few palms that genuinely thrives in shade. Pet safe per ASPCA. Dense growth provides good ground-level nesting cover.

Stately large ornamental palm with a distinctive diamond-pattern trunk and arching silver-green fronds. Small date-like fruits eaten by birds and mammals. Very drought tolerant. Makes a dramatic architectural statement.
warnings: Sharp spine-tipped frond bases can cause serious injury during pruning. Wear heavy gloves and eye protection. Mildly toxic to pets — date palm family seeds can cause neurological issues if ingested in quantity.

plants.description: Very similar to lychee in growing requirements but considered easier and more reliable in South Florida. Fragrant flowers and clusters of tan-skinned sweet fruit. More drought tolerant than lychee once established.

varieties.name: Kohala
varieties.notes: The most widely planted longan in Florida. Very reliable producer, consistent flavor, proven track record in SW Florida.

varieties.name: Biew Kiew
varieties.notes: Thai variety gaining popularity in Florida. Large fruit with excellent sweet flavor.

varieties.name: Edaw
varieties.notes: Early season variety that ripens before Kohala — useful for extending harvest window.

plants.description: Thrives in SW Florida's tropical climate. The world's largest tree fruit — one tree can produce hundreds of lbs per year. Unripe fruit used as a meat substitute. Ripe fruit sweet and tropical.
warnings: Fruit can be very heavy — up to 80 lbs. Plant away from walkways and vehicles. Sticky latex sap is very difficult to remove — use gloves and oil when harvesting.

varieties.name: Black Gold
varieties.notes: Most popular backyard jackfruit in Florida. Soft melting flesh, very sweet, smaller fruit size making harvest easier.

varieties.name: Cheena
varieties.notes: Smaller more manageable tree than standard jackfruit. Good choice for smaller properties.

varieties.name: NS1
varieties.notes: Firm flesh good for cooking as well as fresh eating. Very productive.

plants.description: Essentially a giant herb not a true tree. Extremely fast growing and productive in SW Florida. Hummingbirds visit the flowers. Leaves used for cooking and crafts. Cut down after fruiting and new shoots replace it.

varieties.name: Dwarf Cavendish
varieties.notes: Shorter and more wind resistant than standard Cavendish — better for Cape Coral's storm exposure.

varieties.name: Lady Finger / Sugar banana
varieties.notes: Small finger-sized fruit with exceptionally sweet rich flavor. Thin skin, very sweet.

varieties.name: Ice Cream / Blue Java
varieties.notes: Unique variety with a creamy vanilla-like flavor. Striking blue-silver skin when unripe.

varieties.name: Mysore
varieties.notes: Very disease resistant and productive. Excellent for cooking and fresh eating.

plants.description: One of the most underrated fruit trees for SW Florida. Blooms in fall and winter when almost nothing else does — providing critical nectar for bees. Fruit ripens in late winter to early spring.
warnings: Loquat seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides — seeds are toxic to pets and humans. The flesh is safe but always remove seeds before feeding fruit to pets.

varieties.name: Advance
varieties.notes: Most widely recommended Florida backyard variety. Self-fertile — only one tree needed for fruit.

varieties.name: Big Jim
varieties.notes: Largest fruited commonly available variety. Very sweet, excellent fresh eating quality.

varieties.name: Champagne
varieties.notes: White-fleshed variety with mild sweet flavor. Good consistent production.

plants.description: Beautiful ornamental shade tree that also produces abundantly. The sticky sweet-sour pulp inside the pods is used worldwide in cooking. Very drought tolerant and long-lived. Feathery compound leaves provide dappled shade.

varieties.name: Manila Sweet
varieties.notes: Much sweeter and less acidic than standard tamarind — excellent fresh eating straight from the pod.

varieties.name: Standard / sour tamarind
varieties.notes: Traditional sour cooking variety used in Pad Thai, chutneys, and countless other dishes.

plants.description: A remarkable and genuinely fun fruit tree — the berries contain miraculin, a protein that makes sour foods taste sweet for 30-60 minutes. Small and slow growing — excellent for containers.
warnings: Requires acidic soil — pH 4.5-5.8. Will not thrive in Cape Coral's naturally alkaline soil without significant amendment or container growing.

plants.description: A true South Florida specialty. The salmon-red flesh has a flavor like sweet potato crossed with almond and brown sugar — extraordinary. Very popular in Cuban and Caribbean cuisine. Always buy grafted trees.

varieties.name: Magana
varieties.notes: Most widely grown variety in South Florida. Large fruit, excellent rich flavor, reliable production.

varieties.name: Pantin
varieties.notes: Classic long-established Florida variety. Good reliable flavor and production.

varieties.name: Viejo
varieties.notes: Large fruit with particularly rich flavor. Growing in popularity.

plants.description: Stunning native with brilliant scarlet tubular flower spikes that hummingbirds and butterflies love. Goes dormant in winter but returns vigorously in spring. Thorny stems.
warnings: Seeds are highly toxic to humans and pets — bright red beans in pods are very dangerous if ingested. Plant where children and pets cannot access seed pods.

plants.description: Native evergreen holly with small black berries eaten by bluebirds, robins, and many birds. Excellent for wet areas and low spots. Dense growth provides nesting cover.
warnings: Berries toxic to humans and pets — do not ingest.

plants.description: Spectacular native coastal shrub with long spikes of bright yellow flowers blooming nearly year-round. Extremely salt and drought tolerant — one of the best natives for beachside and coastal properties.
warnings: All parts including seeds are toxic — do not ingest.

plants.description: Excellent native shrub with masses of small white flowers in spring. Small dark fruits eaten by birds. Host plant for spring azure and other butterflies. Can be kept as a compact hedge or small tree. One of the most ecologically valuable native shrubs — seriously underused.

Fast-growing native whose berries are eaten by over 40 bird species. Massive white flower clusters attract bees and butterflies. Cooked berries edible for humans in syrups, jams, and wine. Excellent for wet areas.
warnings: Raw berries, leaves, and stems contain cyanogenic compounds — berries must be cooked before eating. Raw berries can cause nausea in humans and pets.

plants.description: Native coastal shrub producing white to purple plum-like fruits eaten by birds, raccoons, and gopher tortoises. Edible for humans — used in jams and jellies. Very salt and drought tolerant. Excellent hedge plant.
Small native shrub with cheerful yellow flowers blooming nearly year-round. Host plant for cloudless sulphur, sleepy orange, and orange-barred sulphur butterflies. Very drought and salt tolerant.
Native semi-woody shrub and host plant for the federally endangered Bartram's hairstreak butterfly and Florida leafwing butterfly. Very drought tolerant, no irrigation needed once established.
Underused native shrub with tiny black fruits that migrating warblers love. Very salt and drought tolerant. Good informal hedge or naturalistic screen. Fast growing and low maintenance.
Attractive native large shrub or small tree with clusters of small fragrant white flowers loved by hummingbirds, butterflies, and bees. Orange-red fruits eaten by many birds. Very salt tolerant.

Outstanding native coastal shrub with showy white flowers that open at night — fragrant and dramatic. Host plant for Florida white and great southern white butterflies. Attractive red seed pods eaten by birds. Blooms year-round.
One of the most popular flowering shrubs for Southwest Florida. Giant blooms in every color nearly year-round. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit constantly. Flowers are edible for humans.
warnings: Can cause mild vomiting and diarrhea if ingested by pets.

plants.description: Dense clusters of red, orange, pink, or yellow flowers nearly year-round. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit regularly.
warnings: Requires acidic soil — will yellow in alkaline soil. In SW Florida's naturally alkaline soil, amend with sulfur or acidifying fertilizer.

plants.description: Enormously popular foliage shrub for its spectacular coppery-red, orange, and burgundy leaves. Very easy in the heat and humidity. No significant wildlife value but outstanding visual impact year-round.
warnings: Toxic to pets — all parts cause vomiting and skin irritation if ingested.

plants.description: Enormously popular for its spectacular foliage in red, orange, yellow, and green. No significant wildlife value but outstanding visual impact. Very easy in SW Florida's heat.
warnings: Toxic to pets and humans — all parts cause vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation. Milky sap especially irritating.

plants.description: Beautiful sprawling shrub covered in powder-blue flowers nearly year-round. Cassius blue butterfly and other small butterflies use it heavily. Very drought tolerant.
warnings: Sap causes skin irritation. Mildly toxic to pets — can cause vomiting and skin irritation if ingested.

plants.description: Prized for its extraordinarily fragrant white flowers. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers. Requires acidic well-amended soil and afternoon shade to perform well in SW Florida's heat.
warnings: Toxic to pets — causes vomiting, diarrhea, and hives in dogs and cats. Also requires acidic soil — will yellow badly without amendment.

plants.description: Outstanding hummingbird and butterfly shrub with tubular orange-red flowers blooming nearly year-round. Very drought tolerant. Can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a vine. Pet safe.
Beautiful fast-growing shrub with sky-blue flowers and clusters of golden berries. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Birds eat the berries despite their toxicity to mammals.
warnings: Berries toxic to children and pets — can cause fever, seizures, and serious gastrointestinal issues.

plants.description: Attractive native with fragrant yellow-white tubular flowers loved by hummingbirds and butterflies. Distinctive white berries eaten by birds. Very salt and drought tolerant. Underused and underappreciated.

Tough native coastal shrub with large glossy leaves and fragrant white flowers. Berries eaten by birds and mammals. Extremely salt and drought tolerant. Excellent for beachfront and coastal properties.
Native understory shrub with clusters of glossy black berries eagerly eaten by birds. Great for shady spots. Blooms in fall and winter when nectar is scarce.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive coral ardisia (Ardisia crenata) which has serrated leaf edges. Native marlberry has smooth leaf edges.

plants.description: Large native hibiscus with huge pink to white blooms with red centers. Found naturally in marshes, pond edges, and ditches. Velvety silvery-green foliage is attractive even when not in bloom. Deciduous in winter.
Stunning shrub or vine with large brilliant yellow trumpet flowers blooming nearly year-round. Very popular in SW Florida for its striking color.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — causes vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation. Milky sap especially irritating.

plants.description: Extremely popular hedge and privacy shrub in SW Florida. Dense evergreen foliage maintains a tight hedge with minimal pruning. Birds nest in the dense growth.
warnings: Milky sap can cause skin irritation. Mildly toxic to pets if large quantities ingested.

plants.description: Florida's native annual blanket flower with vivid red-orange and yellow daisy-like blooms. Seed heads eaten by birds — leave them standing. Excellent nectar source. Very drought and salt tolerant. Self-seeds readily.
Native low-growing perennial with lavender-purple flowers blooming nearly year-round. Host plant for common buckeye, phaon crescent, and white peacock butterflies. Very adaptable — sun to full shade.
Florida's state wildflower — masses of bright yellow daisy-like blooms in spring. Bees and butterflies visit constantly. Seeds eaten by birds. Self-seeds prolifically.

Stunning native perennial with tall purple flower spikes that bloom from the top down. Butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds visit actively. Seed heads eaten by goldfinches. Blooms in summer and fall when many other flowers are finishing.

Native perennial with fluffy blue-purple flowers that bloom in fall and winter — providing critical late-season nectar. Butterflies and bees swarm it when it blooms. Important gap-filler for late-season pollinator support.

Native coastal goldenrod with large plumes of golden-yellow flowers in fall and winter — one of the most important late-season nectar plants available. Extremely salt and drought tolerant. Essential for year-round wildlife support.

Native perennial with grass-like foliage and charming three-petaled purple-blue flowers. Bees and butterflies visit. Young leaves and flowers edible — used in salads. Naturalizes easily in garden beds.
Non-native host plant for monarchs and queens. Blooms year-round in FL. Best used alongside native milkweeds.
warnings: Non-native milkweed — blooms year-round which may discourage monarch migration south. Plant alongside native Asclepias tuberosa. Mildly toxic to pets in large quantities.

plants.description: Classic reliable annual that blooms year-round in SW Florida. Bees and butterflies visit actively. Strong fragrance deters many garden pests. Flowers edible as a garnish.
warnings: Can cause mild skin irritation and mild gastrointestinal upset in pets if ingested in quantity.

plants.description: One of the best drought-tolerant color plants for SW Florida's full sun areas. Brilliant flowers that close at night and open in sunshine. Very low maintenance — thrives in hot dry spots.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — can cause vomiting and diarrhea if ingested in quantity.

plants.description: The best shade-tolerant annual for color in SW Florida. SunPatiens perform in full sun through shade. Butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds visit.
warnings: Traditional impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) are no longer recommended by UF/IFAS due to invasive risk. Use SunPatiens or New Guinea impatiens varieties only.

plants.description: Striking annual with dramatic plumed or crested flower heads. Butterflies and bees visit actively. Seeds eaten by birds. Leaves and flowers edible. Very heat and drought tolerant. Pet safe.
Large showy daisy-like flowers in bold colors. Bees and butterflies visit. Blooms best in fall through spring in SW Florida — tends to slow in peak summer heat. Pet safe per ASPCA.
Excellent shade-tolerant annual with trumpet-shaped flowers. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit. One of the best choices for shaded flower beds where most annuals refuse to bloom.
Iconic tropical flower with striking orange and blue blooms. Hummingbirds and bees visit. Blooms nearly year-round. Very drought tolerant once established.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — can cause vomiting and nausea if ingested. Seeds are more toxic than flowers.

plants.description: Spectacular foliage plant with enormous heart-shaped leaves in stunning combinations. No significant wildlife value but extraordinary visual impact in shaded areas.
warnings: Highly toxic to pets — all parts cause intense burning and swelling of the mouth, tongue, and throat. Can cause difficulty swallowing and breathing. Serious emergency if ingested.

plants.description: Many non-native salvia varieties perform beautifully alongside the native scarlet sage. Mexican sage, black and blue salvia, and guarani sage all attract hummingbirds and butterflies constantly.

Sprawling coastal native that roots at nodes and stabilizes sandy soil beautifully. Large pink-purple funnel flowers attract bees and butterflies. Handles salt spray, drought, and heat. Excellent for slopes, dunes, and canal banks.

Succulent native groundcover with small pink star flowers nearly year-round. Extremely salt tolerant. Edible leaves with a salty flavor used in salads and cooking. Excellent for coastal properties and canal edges.
Mounding coastal native covered in vivid violet-purple flowers nearly year-round. Butterflies and bees visit constantly. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
Low spreading native coastal groundcover with small pink-white flowers and yellow fruits eaten by birds. Extremely salt and drought tolerant. Forms attractive low mats.
Low spreading native producing small fruits eaten by gopher tortoises, deer, and birds. Spreads by underground runners. Very drought tolerant — great for dry open sunny areas.
Low-growing native of shaded hammock understory with small white flowers and clusters of translucent bright red berries eaten by many birds. One of the best shade-tolerant native groundcovers.

Popular shade-tolerant groundcover forming neat dark green grass-like mounds. No significant wildlife value but excellent for shaded areas. Small white flowers in summer followed by blue-black berries.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — berries can cause vomiting and diarrhea.

plants.description: Versatile clumping groundcover with grass-like foliage and spikes of purple flowers. Dark berries eaten by some birds. Very adaptable to sun through shade.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — berries cause gastrointestinal upset.

plants.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers year-round. Very drought and salt tolerant. Widely planted but a Category 1 invasive in Florida — escapes into natural areas and wetlands.
warnings: Category 1 invasive plant in Florida — escapes easily into natural areas and wetlands. UF/IFAS advises against new plantings. Consider replacing with native beach sunflower or frogfruit.

plants.common_name: Oyster plant / Moses in the cradle
plants.description: Very popular groundcover with striking purple and green sword-shaped leaves. Small white flowers attract bees. Extremely tough and drought tolerant.
warnings: Toxic to pets — sap causes skin irritation and gastrointestinal upset if ingested. Also mildly invasive — listed as Category II invasive by FLEPCC.

plants.description: Low-growing perennial edible groundcover with leaves eaten raw or cooked. Self-roots wherever stems touch ground. Very easy in Southwest Florida's heat. Excellent dual-purpose food garden groundcover.
Colorful edible groundcover with striking purple-backed green leaves. Eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked. Very attractive in shaded beds. Easy and productive in Southwest Florida's warm climate.

Native perennial vine that is a year-round host plant for monarch, queen, AND soldier butterflies — one of the few native milkweed vines in Florida. Clusters of small white flowers attract pollinators.
warnings: Milkweed family — mildly toxic to pets in large quantities.

plants.description: Beautiful native vine with small sky-blue flowers blooming nearly year-round. Excellent nectar source. Very salt and drought tolerant. Well-behaved and not aggressive.
Native vine with enormous fragrant white trumpet flowers that open at dusk. Attracts sphinx moths and other night pollinators. Creates a magical nighttime garden.
warnings: Seeds and leaves are toxic to pets and humans — contain lysergic acid compounds. Keep away from children and pets.

plants.description: Native fruiting vine producing clusters of sweet thick-skinned grapes beloved by birds, raccoons, opossums, and deer. Edible for humans. Host plant for several butterfly species. Excellent dual-purpose food garden vine.
Unusual native vine-like perennial with small lavender-pink daisy flowers that bloom in fall and winter — critically important late-season nectar when most other plants have finished.

Native woody vine with stunning trumpet-shaped orange and red flowers in spring that hummingbirds love. Named for the cross pattern visible in the stem cross-section. Better behaved than trumpet vine.
Stunning tropical vine with distinctive two-toned flowers — white calyx with bright red center. Shade tolerant — excellent for partly shaded fences where few other flowering vines perform.
warnings: Toxic to pets — all parts can cause vomiting and gastrointestinal distress if ingested.

plants.description: Spectacular vine with large sky-blue to lavender trumpet flowers blooming year-round. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit actively. Pet safe.
warnings: Can become invasive — monitor and prevent from escaping into natural areas. Remove seed pods before they mature near conservation areas.

plants.description: Vigorous climbing vine with edible glossy leaves. Tolerates SW Florida's summer heat where cool-season spinach fails. Birds eat the small dark fruits. Productive dual-purpose food and ornamental vine.
Ornamental and edible vine with edible roots and attractive foliage. Host plants for several sphinx moths. Excellent fast-growing groundcover or climbing vine.
Evergreen native vine with intensely fragrant yellow flowers in late winter and spring. Bees and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Drought tolerant and adaptable.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts contain neurotoxins that can cause serious illness or death in humans, pets, and livestock. Never consume any part. Site very carefully around pets and children.

plants.description: Clumping native grass ideal for transitional wet-dry areas and canal edges. Provides dense nesting cover for ground-nesting birds and small mammals. Very salt and flood tolerant.
Delicate native grass with airy purple flower plumes in fall that almost seem to float above the foliage. Seeds eaten by birds. Beautiful mass-planted along sunny borders. Self-seeds readily.

Tall native grass with distinctive golden seed heads that droop to one side. Seeds eaten by many birds. Host plant for several skipper butterfly species. Good structural backdrop in naturalistic plantings.

Native grass that turns brilliantly russet-copper in fall and winter — stunning seasonal color. Fluffy seed heads eaten by birds. Host plant for several skipper butterflies. Tolerates both dry and moist conditions.
The iconic grass of the Everglades. Seeds and structure provide critical habitat for wading birds, rails, and small mammals. Very appropriate for canal edges and wet naturalistic areas.
warnings: Extremely sharp serrated leaf edges cause serious cuts — handle with heavy gloves and long sleeves. Not appropriate near play spaces.

plants.description: Tall cane grass producing sweet edible stalks. The thick straight dried canes make excellent garden stakes. Birds nest in the dense clumps.
warnings: Spreads by rhizomes — give it a contained dedicated spot away from natural areas.

plants.description: Clumping bamboo provides excellent privacy screening and nesting habitat. Canes harvested for garden stakes of any size. Young shoots of some species edible.
warnings: CRITICAL: Only plant clumping varieties. Running bamboo (Phyllostachys spp.) is highly invasive in Florida and nearly impossible to eradicate.

plants.description: Low-growing native rush-like plant that forms dense mats in shallow water. Seeds eaten by waterfowl and wading birds. Excellent fish habitat and spawning cover. Very important for stabilizing canal and pond edges.

Native emergent grass that forms extensive colonies in shallow water and wet soil. Seeds eaten by waterfowl. Dense colonies provide nesting habitat and fish spawning cover. Essential for canal bank stabilization.
Native yellow pond lily with distinctive cup-shaped yellow flowers. Dense pads shade water reducing algae. Seeds and roots eaten by ducks, fish, and mammals. Tolerates some shade.

Spectacular native lotus with enormous pale yellow flowers. Seeds heavily eaten by ducks and waterfowl. Edible — seeds, roots, and young leaves all eaten historically. Spreads aggressively — best in larger ponds.

Native submerged aquatic plant forming dense masses underwater — one of the most important native aquatic plants for fish habitat. Provides critical spawning cover. Waterfowl eat the plant material. Helps filter water.
Native submerged grass with long ribbon-like leaves — a critical component of healthy freshwater and brackish water ecosystems. Provides essential fish habitat, manatee forage, and duck food.
Asian lotus grown for its stunning large flowers in pink and white. Edible — roots widely used in Asian cooking, seeds eaten as snacks, young leaves edible. Well suited to SW Florida's warm climate.
Large-leafed tropical plant grown for its edible starchy corms — a staple crop in Pacific and Asian cuisines. Thrives in wet to boggy conditions and partial shade.
warnings: All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals — toxic raw. Must be thoroughly cooked before eating. Also toxic to pets — causes intense burning and swelling of mouth and throat.

plants.description: One of the top hummingbird plants in North America. Brilliant scarlet flower spikes are irresistible to hummingbirds. Excellent for canal edges and wet areas in Southwest Florida.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets if ingested in quantity — contains alkaloids causing vomiting and paralysis.

plants.description: Native canna with large showy yellow flowers that hummingbirds love. Tolerates both wet and seasonally dry conditions making it versatile for wet edges and rain gardens.

Small native air plant forming distinctive ball-like clusters on branches. Produces small blue to violet flowers. Bees visit the flowers. Provides microhabitat for insects and spiders. Common on live oaks throughout SW Florida.

Florida's largest native bromeliad — can reach 6-12 ft tall when in flower. Tank bromeliad whose enormous central cup creates a small ecosystem. Hummingbirds visit the flowering spike. Blooms only once then dies (monocarpic).
warnings: Endangered — protected by Florida law. Only purchase from licensed nurseries. Monocarpic — blooms once then dies, may take 10-20 years to bloom.

plants.description: Common native tillandsia forming dense clusters of needle-like leaves. Violet flower stalks bloom in spring. Found in hammocks and swamps throughout Lee and Collier counties.
Distinctive native tillandsia with twisted banded leaves and spectacular red and pink flower bracts. Found naturally in Southwest Florida's mangrove and hammock habitats.
warnings: Endangered — protected by Florida law. Purchase only from licensed nurseries.

plants.description: Native epiphytic orchid with unusual upside-down shell-shaped purple and green flowers that bloom nearly year-round. One of Florida's most distinctive native orchids. Available from specialty native plant nurseries.
plants.mount_method: Mount on cork bark or hardwood

plants.description: Large and impressive native orchid with spectacular yellow and brown flower spikes. One of Florida's largest native orchids. Threatened by habitat loss and collecting.
warnings: Threatened species — purchase only from licensed nurseries. Never collect from the wild.
plants.mount_method: Mount on large branches or cork

plants.description: Native epiphytic fern with long grass-like fronds that cascade from palm boots and tree bark. Common on cabbage palms throughout SW Florida. Part of the authentic Southwest Florida canopy ecosystem.
plants.mount_method: Self-establishes on palm boots and bark

plants.description: Non-native bromeliads grown for spectacular foliage and flower displays. Water-holding tanks attract hummingbirds and bees. Available in an extraordinary range of colors and forms.
warnings: Some cultivated bromeliad species have sharp leaf margins. Mildly irritating sap in some species. Not severely toxic but monitor pets around the water-holding cups.
plants.mount_method: Containers, wood mounts, or tree forks

plants.description: Extraordinary tree-like cactus native to the Florida Keys and extreme South Florida — considered one of the rarest cacti on earth with fewer than 100 wild plants remaining. Bright yellow-green flowers attract hummingbirds and bees.
warnings: Critically endangered — considered the rarest cactus in the world outside of cultivation. Protected by federal and state law. Purchase only from nurseries legally propagating specimens.

plants.description: Dramatic native yucca with razor-sharp spine-tipped leaves and tall spikes of creamy white flowers. Hummingbirds and bees visit. Fruits and seeds eaten by birds. Very salt and drought tolerant. Bold architectural statement plant.
warnings: Toxic to pets — contains saponins causing vomiting, diarrhea, and lethargy. The extremely sharp leaf tips also cause serious puncture wounds. Keep well away from pet play areas.

plants.description: More manageable native yucca with gracefully recurving leaves that lack the lethal sharp tips of Spanish bayonet. Tall creamy flower spikes attract hummingbirds and bees.
warnings: Toxic to pets — same saponin compounds as other yuccas causing vomiting and diarrhea.

plants.description: Tall columnar cactus producing large fragrant night-blooming white flowers and edible red-skinned fruits. Fast growing — can reach 15-30 ft. Very drought tolerant. Pet safe.
warnings: Night-blooming — large fragrant white flowers open only at night attracting moths and bats. Spines are significant — handle with care.

plants.description: Dramatic large agave living for decades then producing a spectacular 15-30 ft flowering spike once before dying. Hummingbirds, bees, and orioles attracted to the flowers. Produces offsets that continue the colony.
warnings: Sharp terminal spines on leaf tips cause serious puncture wounds. Keep away from foot traffic areas. Mildly toxic — sap causes skin irritation. The flowering spike (15-30 ft) can fall without warning.

plants.description: Shrubby succulent with small rounded edible leaves. One of the few truly pet safe and edible succulents. Very drought tolerant. Can be grown as a sprawling groundcover, upright shrub, or trained as a bonsai.
One of the best shade-tolerant succulents. Striking zebra-stripe banding. Pet safe per ASPCA. No significant wildlife value. Excellent for containers and shaded patios.
Cheerful succulent with bright clusters of flowers in red, orange, yellow, and pink. Bees and butterflies visit. Blooms in winter and spring.
