warnings: Toxic to pets — on ASPCA top ten most toxic plant list. Contains cardiac glycosides causing serious heart rhythm abnormalities in dogs and cats. Can be fatal in significant doses.

plants.description: Classic long-lived succulent with thick glossy leaves and a tree-like form over time. Very drought tolerant. Easy in Southwest Florida. No significant wildlife value.
warnings: Toxic to pets — causes vomiting, lethargy, coordination problems, and slowed heart rate in dogs and cats.

plants.description: One of the most widespread ferns in the world and a native of Florida's flatwoods. Provides cover for ground-nesting birds. Very drought tolerant — the most sun-tolerant native fern in SW Florida. Spreads aggressively via rhizomes.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets and livestock if consumed in large quantities over time. Spreads very aggressively — plant in contained areas.

plants.description: Delicate and beautiful native fern with distinctive fan-shaped leaflets on wiry black stems. Thrives in humid shaded areas with good moisture. Excellent for containers and shaded patios.
Robust native fern with bold upright fronds. Evergreen in Southwest Florida's mild climate. More drought tolerant than many shade ferns. Excellent for rain gardens and moist shaded areas.

Native fern with glossy dark green arching fronds forming attractive colonies in wet areas. Adaptable — tolerates both shade and full sun if moisture is adequate. Excellent for naturalizing canal banks.

Majestic native fern producing large vase-shaped clumps with bold textured fronds. Birds use the fibrous root mass for nesting material. The fertile fronds produce russet-brown spore masses that look like flowers. Very long-lived.
Very popular ornamental for its distinctive cylindrical plume-like fronds. Extremely drought tolerant. Not a true fern despite its name.
warnings: Toxic to pets — berries and all parts cause vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain in dogs and cats. The related asparagus fern (Asparagus aethiopicus) is invasive — foxtail fern is the safe non-invasive variety.

plants.description: Popular non-native fern widely used by florists. Excellent shade-tolerant groundcover. Pet safe per ASPCA. Slow to establish but very long-lived. Doesn't spread aggressively.
Large ornamental ginger relative with edible rhizomes widely used in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking. Spectacular white and red flowers attract bees and hummingbirds. Very ornamental and productive.
Stunning ornamental ginger with large intensely fragrant white flowers that hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies adore. One of the most fragrant plants available.
warnings: Can become invasive in wet areas near natural streams — monitor spread.

plants.description: Spectacular ornamental ginger with bold red cone-shaped flower bracts that bloom nearly year-round. Hummingbirds and bees visit constantly. Small plantlets form on flower heads and can be propagated easily.
One of the most productive food crops in the tropics. Large starchy roots cooked like potatoes. The tall straight dried canes are excellent garden stakes. Plant from stem cuttings.
warnings: Must be cooked before eating — raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds toxic to humans and pets. Always boil, roast, or fry thoroughly.

plants.description: Striking non-native bulb with brilliant red spider-like flowers that emerge on bare stalks in fall — often right after a hurricane or heavy rain. Hummingbirds and bees visit.
warnings: All parts highly toxic to pets and humans — contain lycorine and other alkaloids. Bulbs especially dangerous.

plants.description: Heat-loving perennial rhizome that thrives in SW Florida's climate. Large tropical blooms nearly year-round. Edible rhizomes used like arrowroot. Pet safe per ASPCA.
Round bright green leaves that pop up in lawns and wet areas. Edible leaves used in Asian cuisine and as a nutritious tea. Bees and small butterflies visit the tiny flowers. Indicates moist soil.
plants.management: Can be eaten or let grow in wet areas. If you want a dry lawn, improve drainage rather than spray.

plants.description: Low spreading native with small white flowers common in moist lawn areas. Bees visit the flowers. Indicates wet soil conditions. Part of the native lawn ecosystem.
plants.management: Tolerate in lawn areas with moisture issues — indicates drainage problems better addressed by soil improvement than herbicide.

plants.description: Small white-flowered native lawn weed. Bees and small butterflies visit the flowers continuously. Very common in SW Florida lawns. Low growing and doesn't compete aggressively with turf.
plants.management: Tolerate in lawn areas — flowers provide real pollinator value for minimal visual impact.

plants.description: Small white-pink flowers bloom nearly year-round. Bees and butterflies visit actively. Very common but genuinely useful as a pollinator plant in areas with limited other resources.
Small native herb that volunteers in garden beds and shaded areas. Bees visit the tiny flowers. Seeds eaten by birds. Used medicinally in traditional herbalism.
plants.management: Tolerate in shaded areas. Easy to pull if it appears where unwanted.

plants.description: Thorny plant with white flowers and tomato-like fruits. Toxic to pets and livestock. Federally listed noxious weed. Gets mistaken for a benign weed — it is not.
warnings: Federally listed noxious weed. Toxic to pets and livestock. Report infestations to FDACS.
plants.management: REMOVE IMMEDIATELY. Report to FDACS. Do not confuse with native nightshades.

plants.description: Aggressive vine that grows up to 8 inches per day, smothering trees and shrubs. Produces aerial potato-like bulbils that fall and sprout. Extremely difficult to eradicate.
warnings: Toxic potato-like bulbils dangerous to pets. Grows 8 inches per day.
plants.management: REMOVE IMMEDIATELY. Collect ALL bulbils. See Invasive category for full removal guidance.

plants.description: Australian tree planted widely for landscaping and erosion control that now invades natural areas throughout South Florida. Forms dense monocultures displacing native vegetation. Ironically still sold at some nurseries.
warnings: Produces thousands of seeds that persist in soil for years. Removal requires sustained multi-year follow-up.
plants.removal_method: Cut and treat stump with triclopyr immediately. Resprouts vigorously — treat every resprout. Produces enormous seed banks in the soil — seedlings will emerge for years.

plants.description: Common houseplant and outdoor landscaping tree that has escaped into natural hammocks and disturbed areas, displacing native vegetation. Produces masses of red berries spread by birds.
warnings: Toxic to pets — all parts cause oral irritation, vomiting, and excessive drooling. Widely sold as a houseplant.
plants.removal_method: Cut and treat stump with herbicide immediately. Resprouting vigorous. Remove all seedlings as they appear.
